body.p: The Final Office Action mailed August 23, 2023 (hereinafter "Final Office Action") has been carefully reviewed, and Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration of the rejections of Applicant's claims, particularly in view of the foregoing amendments and the remarks that follow.
Claims 1 and 4-13 were previously pending. By the present submission, claims 1, 10, and 13 have been amended, while no claims are newly cancelled or added herein.

In claim 1, two instances of the word "only" have been added. In particular, the phrases "transmit a control signal" and "transmit the upper wheel speed limit" have been replaced with "transmit only a control signal" and "transmit only the upper when speed limit," respectively. Amended claim 1 defines that only the upper wheel speed limit is transmitted when the desired torque is above zero, and only the lower wheel speed limit is transmitted when the desired torque is below zero.
Claims 10 and 13 have been amended in a manner similar to claim 1.

In claim 10, two instances of the word "only" have been added. In particular, the text "an upper wheel speed limit received from the vehicle motion management system when the desired torque is above zero, and a lower wheel speed limit received from the vehicle motion management system when the desired torque is below zero" has been replaced with "an upper wheel speed limit received from the vehicle motion management system only when the desired torque is above zero, and a lower wheel speed limit received from the vehicle motion management system only when the desired torque is below zero."

In claim 13, two instances of the word "only" have been added. In particular, the text "the wheel speed limit comprises an upper wheel speed limit determined when the desired torque is above zero, and a lower wheel speed limit determined when the desired torque is below zero" has been replaced with "the wheel speed limit comprises an upper wheel speed limit determined only when the desired torque is above zero, and a lower wheel speed limit determined only when the desired torque is below zero."

The foregoing amendments to the claims are supported by at least page 3, lines 26-31 and page 15, lines 4-10 of the present application. From these portions of the application, a person of ordinary skill in the art will directly and unambiguously understand that the lower wheel speed limit is not transmitted when the desired torque is above zero, and the upper wheel speed limit is not transmitted when the desired toque is below zero.

The amendments to Applicant's claims are fully supported by and consistent with the originally-filed application. No new matter within the meaning of 35 U.S.C. § 132(a) and 37 C.F.R. § 1.121 has been introduced by the foregoing amendments.

body.p: A request for consideration (Form PTO/SB/434) under the After Final Consideration Pilot 2.0 (AFCP 2.0) is filed herewith. In cases where a narrowing amendment is made to at least one independent claim, AFCP 2.0 authorizes additional time for the Examiner to search and/or consider amendments after final rejection as well as to schedule and conduct an interview to discuss the results of their search and/or consideration with Applicant's representative when the response does not place the application in condition for allowance. This application is eligible for consideration under the AFCP 2.0 program due to the narrowing amendments made herein to independent claims 1, 10, and 13.

Applicant respectfully disagrees with the foregoing rejections in application to the claims as amended herein for at least the reasons set out below.

In order for an obviousness rejection to be appropriate, a prior art reference (or references when combined) must typically disclose all of the claim limitations.1 Additionally, "there must be some articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning to support the legal conclusion of obviousness" to establish obviousness.2

The Supreme Court has confirmed that references that teach away from the invention are evidence of the non-obviousness of a claimed invention, and reaffirmed the principle that a fact finder judging patentability "should be aware, of course, of the distortion caused by hindsight bias and must be cautious of arguments reliant upon ex post reasoning."3

Following KSR, the Federal Circuit held that although "rigid" application of the TSM test for obviousness is improper, application of a flexible TSM test remains the primary guarantee against improper "hindsight" analysis, because a flexibly applied TSM test ensures that the obviousness analysis proceeds on the basis of evidence in existence before time the application

1 MPEP § 2143.03; Arendi S.A.R.L. v. Apple Inc., 832 F.3d 1355, 1362 (Fed. Cir. 2016) (use of common sense to supply a limitation missing from the prior art" must be supported by substantial evidence and reasoned explanation, not conclusory generalizations).
2 KSR Int'l v. Teleflex, Inc., 550 U.S. 398, 418, 82 USPQ.2d 1385, 1396 (2007).
3 KSR, 82 USPQ2d at 1395, 1399.
was filed, as required by 35 U.S.C. § 103.4
A suggestion to combine references cannot require substantial reconstruction or redesign
of such references, or a change in basic operating principles of a construction of a reference, to
considered in its entirety, including portions that teach away from the invention under
consideration. Simply stated, the prior art must be considered as a whole.6 "It is impermissible
within the framework of section 103 to pick and choose from any one reference only so much of
it as will support a given position, to the exclusion of other parts necessary to the full appreciation
of what such reference fairly suggests to one of ordinary skill in the art."7 The Federal Circuit and
its predecessor court have repeatedly held that if references taken in combination would produce
a "seemingly inoperative" device, then such references teach away from the combination and
cannot serve as predicates for aprimafacie case of obviousness.'
The Federal Circuit has reaffirmed the necessity of avoiding hindsight bias when
considering whether a claim may be obvious, noting specifically that a proper obviousness analysis
"requires a form of amnesia that 'forgets' the invention and analyzes the prior art and
understanding of the problem at the date of invention."9

See also MPEP 2143.01 ("If the proposed modification or combination of the prior art would change the principle of operation of the prior art invention being modified, then the teachings of the references are not sufficient to render the claims prima facie obvious.')
6 W.L. Gore & Associates, Inc. v. Garlock, Inc., 721 F.2d 1540, 220 USPQ 303 (Fed. Cir. 1983), cert. denied, 469 U.S. 851 (1984); MPEP § 2141.02.

7 Application of Wesslau, 353 F.2d 238, 241 (C.C.P.A. 1965); Bausch & Lomb, Inc. v. Barnes-Hind/Hydrocurve, 796 F.2d 443, 448 (Fed. Cir. 1986), cert. denied, 484 U.S. 823 (1987). 8McGinley v. Franklin Sports, Inc., 262 F.3d 1339, 60 USPQ2d 1001, 1010 (Fed. Cir. 2001); Tec Alr, Inc. v. Denso Mfg. Mch. Inc., 192 F.3d 1353, 52 USPQ2d 1294, 1298 (Fed. Cir. 1999) (proposed combination of references that would be inoperable for intended purpose supports teaching away from combination); In re Gordon, 733 F.2d 900, 902, 221 USPQ 1125, 1127 (Fed. Cir. 1984) (inoperable modification teaches away); In re Sponnoble, 405 F.2d 578, 587, 160 USPQ 237, 244 (C.C.P.A. 1969) (references teach away from combination if combination produces seemingly inoperative device).

9 See Mintz v. Dietz & Watson, 679 F.3d 1372, 1379 (Fed. Cir. 2012) ("Simply because the technology can be easily understood does not mean that it will satisfy the legal standard of obviousness. In fact, objective consideration of simple technology is often the most difficult because, once the problem and solution appear together in the patent disclosure, the advance seems self-evident. Instead, the proper analysis requires a form of amnesia that 'forgets' the invention and analyzes the prior art and understanding of the problem at the date of invention.")

p.u: and Its Dependents over Ford and Suhre

body.p: Ford discloses a traction control system for a vehicle having a first wheel driven by a first electric motor having a first set of coil windings and a first controller arranged to control current in the coil windings for generating a drive torque for driving the first wheel, and a second controller arranged to determine a maximum wheel velocity and a minimum wheel velocity. (Ford, Abstract.) The second controller communicates to the first controller the maximum and minimum values and a torque demand value. (Ford, Abstract.)

In connection with the rejection of claim 1, page 7 of the Office Action conceded that Ford does not disclose determining the speed limit based on the desired torque; however, page 8 of the Office Action pointed to Suhre (e.g., Col. 8, lines 3-5 and Col. 3, lines 20-25 thereof) as disclosing the slip ratio being determined as function of tractive force command (received for the accelerator pedal of the driven vehicle), such that page 8 of the Office Action contended that one of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to combine Suhre with Ford in "order to include the motion request in the computation of speed limit and thereby yield outputs better suited to the specific motion request made by the driver of the vehicle."

Further in connection with the rejection of claim 1, page 6 of the Office Action pointed to paragraphs [0061] and [0062] of Ford as disclosing sending maximum and minimum speed limit values, as well as individual torque demand requests, to each motor, and the same page of the Office Action pointed to "Paragraph 0061 [of Ford as] disclosing speed limits comprising upper and lower speed limits."

Page 3 of the Office Action acknowledged Applicant's argument raised in the reply filed on May 24, 2023 that the claimed invention involves "sending only the upper limit or only the lower limit," but indicated that "[t]he invention as claimed does not recite in the independent claim sending [transmitting] only the upper limit or lower limit in response to the desired torque being above or below zero" wherein 'sending both an upper and lower speed limit in response to a determination of the desired torque being, for example, above zero still fulfills the [claimed] criteri[a] ... transmit the upper wheel speed limit to the motion support system when the desired torque is above zero ... [and] transmit the lower when speed limit to the motion support system when the desired torque is below zero."
To address the foregoing contentions by the Examiner, claim 1 has been amended herein

to define that only the upper wheel speed limit is transmitted when the desired torque is above zero, and only the lower wheel speed limit is transmitted when the desired torque is below zero. (Corresponding amendments have also been made to claims 10 and 13.) Such amendments distinguish the disclosures of the cited references. Neither Ford nor Suhre discloses or provides any derivative basis for transmitting only the upper wheel speed limit when the desired torque is above zero, and transmitting only the lower wheel speed limit when the desired torque is below zero.

As disclosed by the present application, by using the vehicle motion management system, (i.e., the upper layer control module) to determine if only an upper speed limit or only a lower speed limit should be transmitted to the motion support system (i.e., the lower layer control module), will substantially reduce the data bandwidth in the data sent between these modules.

Thus, sending only the upper limit or only or lower limit, will, contrary to the Examiner's opinion expressed in the February 23, 2023 Office Action, meaningfully affect the operation of the system, as the response time will be even further reduced (and therefore improved).

Additionally, by letting the vehicle motion management system discriminate between a torque level above or below zero, and transmitting a specific wheel speed limit based on this determination, will beneficially enable a simplified motion support system to be employed. Conversely, in the system according to Ford (whether or not combined with Suhre), the control devices 400 at the wheels must be programmed to enable positive and negative torque to be distinguished, and the control devices 400 use different wheel speed limits based on this determination. Turning back to the present case, the vehicle motion management system of claim 1 is connectable to a motion support system that uses the wheel speed limit the motion support system is instructed to use, such that the motion support system does not need to make any active decisions.

Moreover, the control unit 102 according to Ford is not disclosed as being able to transmit different wheel speed limits based on a positive torque (i.e., torque above zero) or negative torque (i.e., torque below zero), according to the final two clauses of amended claim 1.

Thus, the solution described in Ford will exhibit a slower response (e.g., due to increased bandwidth requirements), require additional programming, and exhibit reduced functionality, in comparison to the vehicle motion management system (coupleable to a motion support system)
the present invention. Suhre fails to remedy the deficiency of Ford in disclosing every feature of amended claim 1.
For at least the foregoing reasons, the subject matter of amended claim 1 is patentably distinguished over the hypothetical combination of Ford and Suhre.

Since dependent claims inherently include the features of the claims on which they depend, claims 5, 7 and 8 (which depend from claim 1) are patentably distinguished over Ford and Suhre for at least the same reasons articulated above in connection with claim 1. Accordingly, it is not necessary to address the additional features in dependent claims 5, 7, and 8 to overcome the rejections of such claims; however, Applicant reserves the right to do so in the future, if necessary.
